claims.text: The initial HEA multilayers have coherent interfaces and primarily exhibit diffusion-mediated creep at high temperature.
Introducing a thin Nb interlayer increases interface coherency.
The Nb-induced increase in interface coherency shifts the dominant high-temperature creep mechanism from diffusion-mediated to dislocation-mediated creep.
Nb can be used as an ultrathin, adjustable-thickness refractory interlayer in the HEA multilayer stack.
The relevant transition can be tested at approximately 600–700 °C under controlled applied stress.
Both diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep may be active under the proposed testing conditions.
The Nb interlayer has a lattice parameter intermediate between those of the adjacent HEA layers.
An intermediate Nb lattice parameter reduces lattice mismatch and modifies local interfacial strain fields.
Changes in lattice matching can modify dislocation behavior in an HEA.
Adjusting Nb interlayer thickness increases the activation energy for diffusion through enhanced interface coherency.
The increased diffusion activation energy suppresses vacancy diffusion and diffusion-mediated creep.
The Nb-modified interface facilitates dislocation glide or climb.
Modified atomic bonding and lattice matching at the interface cause the creep-mechanism transition.
Adding the Nb interlayer will measurably decrease the creep rate associated with diffusion-dominated deformation.
Adding the Nb interlayer will produce evidence of dislocation-mediated slip, including increased dislocation structures or slip-band formation.
HEA multilayers without the Nb interlayer primarily exhibit diffusion-mediated creep under comparable high-temperature stress conditions.
The influence of the Nb interlayer depends on its thickness and processing conditions.
Excessive Nb thickness or loss of interface coherency outside the tested temperature range could negate the intended effect.
The magnitude of the activation-energy shift and the optimal Nb interlayer thickness have not yet been determined.
